title: Unitriangular unipotence is invariant under field extension
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. All groups are affine $k$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Unipotent means admitting a closed group immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion] into some $\mathcal U_{n,k}\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_{n,k}$, $n\geq1$ [def-sc-general-linear-group], where $\mathcal U_{n,k}(A)$ consists of upper triangular matrices with diagonal entries $1$ for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$. Let $K/k$ be any field extension [def-pc-field-extension], and write $G_K=G\times_{\operatorname{Spec}k}\operatorname{Spec}K$ for scalar extension [def-pc-base-change]. Then $G$ is unipotent over $k$ if and only if $G_K$ is unipotent over $K$. Neither field is required to be perfect, and $G$ need not be smooth or connected.

source.place: Corollary 14.9, printed p.282, together with Theorem 14.5(a),(b), printed pp.281--282. This statement uses closed unitriangular immersions, not only unipotence of geometric points.

proof.text: Suppose first that $i:G\hookrightarrow\mathcal U_{n,k}$ is a closed group immersion. Its scalar extension is a closed immersion by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-base-change]. It is still a group homomorphism: base changing the group-law diagrams preserves their equalities. For any commutative $K$-algebra $R$, the points of $(\mathcal U_{n,k})_K$ are exactly the same upper unitriangular matrices over $R$ as those of $\mathcal U_{n,K}$. More explicitly, its coordinate ring is $K\otimes_k k[x_{ij}:i<j]=K[x_{ij}:i<j]$, with multiplication given by $(XY)_{ij}=X_{ij}+Y_{ij}+\sum_{i<l<j}X_{il}Y_{lj}$. The affine fibre-product and tensor-pushout statements [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra, lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property] give this identification and its compatibility with multiplication. Thus $i_K$ realizes unipotence over $K$.

source.place: Corollary 14.9, printed p.282, forward implication, using the equivalent unitriangular realization in Theorem 14.5(b).

proof.text: Now assume $G_K$ has a closed unitriangular immersion. Every nonzero finite-dimensional rational representation $V$ of $G$ has a nonzero rational fixed vector over $k$. Indeed choose a basis of $V$ by [lem-weil-pbc-vector-space-basis-through-vector], writing $V=k^d$, $d\geq1$. Scalar extension gives a rational representation on $V\otimes_kK=K^d$. Here $G_K$ is affine of finite type: the algebra $k[G]$ has finitely many generators by [lem-pc-affine-finite-type-algebra]; if it is generated by $a_1,\ldots,a_s$, its scalar extension is generated over $K$ by $a_i\otimes1$, by [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra] and the definition [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Apply [lem-sfb-unitriangular-subgroup-rational-fixed-vector] over $K$ to obtain a nonzero vector fixed over every $K$-algebra. Apply [lem-sfb-rational-fixed-space-base-change] with $H=G$ and scalar algebra $A=K$. The identity realizes $G$ as a closed subgroup of itself. Its comparison identifies that nonzero vector with an element of $V^G\otimes_kK$. If $V^G=0$, every pure tensor in this tensor product is zero, hence the tensor product is zero by [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product], a contradiction. Thus $V^G\ne0$, with invariance over all $k$-algebras, not just field-valued points.

source.place: Corollary 14.9, printed p.282, converse; Proposition 4.31 and Corollary 4.34, printed pp.96--97; Theorem 14.5(b) implies (a), printed pp.281--282.

proof.text:
We prove by induction on $d\geq1$ that every $d$-dimensional rational representation of $G$ has a basis in which its action on every algebra is upper unitriangular. Choose a nonzero rational fixed vector $v$ by step 2, and extend $v$ to a basis by [lem-weil-pbc-vector-space-basis-through-vector], placing it first. For $d=1$ the action is the identity over every algebra, proving the base case. For $d>1$, in this basis the representing matrix, over every $k$-algebra $R$, has the block form
$$r_R(g)=\begin{pmatrix}1&b_R(g)\\0&M_R(g)\end{pmatrix}.$$
Its inverse has the same first column, since it is $r_R(g^{-1})$. Multiplying these two block matrices gives that $M_R(g)$ is invertible. Block multiplication also gives $M_R(gh)=M_R(g)M_R(h)$, and naturality follows entry by entry from that of $r$. Thus these matrices give a natural representation on $R^{d-1}$, the action on $V/kv$. The finite-dimensional clause of [lem-sfb-rational-representation-comodule-dictionary] makes it a rational representation $G\to\mathrm{GL}_{d-1,k}$. This construction uses all algebra-valued points, so applies equally to nonreduced groups.

source.place: Proposition 14.3, printed p.280: explicit fixed-line induction in place of choosing a composition series; Remark 4.1, printed p.84, for the natural representation.

proof.text: Apply the induction hypothesis from step 3 to the $(d-1)$-dimensional quotient representation. It gives a $k$-basis of $V/kv$ whose matrices over every $R$ are upper unitriangular. Lift this basis to $V$ and put $v$ first. These vectors form a basis: projecting a linear relation kills all quotient coefficients, then kills the coefficient of $v$; and subtracting a lift of the quotient expansion leaves a multiple of $v$. In the resulting block matrix the lower-right block is upper unitriangular, the lower-left block is zero, and the first diagonal entry is $1$. Therefore the whole matrix is upper unitriangular. This completes the induction for every finite positive $d$.

source.place: Proposition 14.3, printed p.280, fixed-vector construction of a full flag with trivial one-dimensional quotients.

proof.text: Take the closed faithful representation $\rho:G\hookrightarrow\mathrm{GL}_{m,k}$, $m\geq1$, provided by [lem-sfb-affine-group-faithful-linear-representation]. Steps 3--4 give a basis in which all its algebra-valued matrices are upper unitriangular. Changing basis preserves closedness: conjugation by a constant $C\in\mathrm{GL}_m(k)$ is a scheme automorphism, with coordinate substitutions $X\mapsto C^{-1}XC$ and inverse $X\mapsto CXC^{-1}$ in the coordinate algebra of [def-sc-general-linear-group]; their composites fix every matrix entry and the inverted determinant. Equivalently their ring maps are inverse, so composing the coordinate surjection of $\rho$ with this automorphism is surjective by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-affine-cover-criterion]. Denote the conjugated closed representation again by $\rho$.

source.place: Theorem 14.5(a) implies (b), printed p.281; Theorem 4.9, printed p.87, followed by Proposition 14.3, printed p.280.

proof.text: Write $B=k[G]$ and $P=k[x_{ij},\det(X)^{-1}]=k[\mathrm{GL}_{m,k}]$ as in [def-sc-general-linear-group]. The map $f:P\to B$ of $\rho$ is surjective by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-affine-cover-criterion]. Evaluate the unitriangular identity of step 5 at the universal point $\mathrm{id}_B\in G(B)$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. This gives $f(x_{ij})=0$ for $i>j$ and $f(x_{ii})=1$. Thus $f$ kills the ideal $J=(x_{ij}\ (i>j),x_{ii}-1)$ and the well-defined map $[p]\mapsto f(p)$ factors it through $P/J=k[x_{ij}:i<j]=k[\mathcal U_{m,k}]$: the determinant becomes $1$ in this quotient. The induced ring map $P/J\to B$ is surjective since $f$ is. The same affine criterion therefore makes $G\to\mathcal U_{m,k}$ a closed immersion. On every algebra its matrices are those of $\rho$, so it respects multiplication, identity and inverse. This is the required closed group immersion over $k$, proving the converse.

source.place: Theorem 14.5(a) implies (b), printed p.281, with the closed-immersion check made explicit; affine criterion: Stacks Tag 01QO, morphisms-lemma-closed-immersion.

lean.note: Both sides express a closed subgroup embedding in GL_n, n>0, satisfying the unitriangular equations on every commutative test algebra. This is exactly a closed embedding in U_n. Scalar extension is Over.pullback.mapGrp, with the canonical pulled-back group law. The smooth-only SolvableGroupStructure.IsUnipotent is deliberately inapplicable; no smoothness or perfectness hypothesis is imposed.
